h1: Beer styles that pair with a Bengali meal, fish to mishti
title: Beer With a Bengali Meal | Craft Beer School
desc: Beer styles that suit a Bengali meal, from shorshe ilish and macher jhol to kosha mangsho and mishti doi, with pairing logic you can reuse.
teaser: Mustard oil, sweet fish curries, slow cooked mutton and then mishti. Here is which beer to pour at each stage.
standfirst: A Bengali meal moves in a clear order, from bitter to sweet. That order makes beer pairing easier than you might think. Here is what to pour with each course and why it works.
sections:
A traditional Bengali meal runs in sequence: something bitter like shukto, then dal and fried vegetables, then fish, then meat, then chutney, then sweets. Each stage has a dominant flavour, so you can match a beer to it rather than finding one bottle to fight the whole table.

Two ingredients drive most of the choices. Mustard oil and ground mustard give a nasal heat that rises rather than burns. Sugar shows up in more savoury dishes than outsiders expect. Carbonation cuts through mustard oil well. Sweetness needs a beer with some malt behind it, or the beer tastes thin and sour by comparison. The Indian food and beer pairing guide covers these principles across regions.

Shukto is a mild, slightly bitter vegetable stew with bitter gourd, milk and poppy or mustard. Pair it with something gentle: a helles or a light kölsch. Avoid hoppy beers here, because hop bitterness stacks on top of bitter gourd and the result is harsh.

With dal and crisp fried begun bhaja or aloo bhaja, a pilsner works well. Its bitterness and fizz scrub the oil from your palate between bites.
Fish: macher jhol and shorshe ilish

Macher jhol is a light, thin fish curry with potato, turmeric and often ginger or cumin. A witbier suits it: coriander and orange peel in the beer echo the spices, while its soft wheat body matches the delicate fish.

Shorshe ilish, hilsa steamed or cooked in a sharp mustard paste, is the big test. Hilsa is oily and bony, the mustard is pungent and green chillies add heat. A hefeweizen is our first choice. High carbonation lifts the oil, the banana and clove esters stand up to mustard and the low bitterness avoids clashing with the chilli. A crisp Czech style pale lager is a good second.

Chingri malai curry, prawns in coconut milk, is rich and slightly sweet. A Belgian blonde or a saison brings enough body and spice to match it.

Kosha mangsho is mutton cooked slowly until the masala darkens and clings to the meat. It is deep, oniony and only moderately hot. This is where darker beers come in. An amber ale, a Vienna lager or an English brown ale has caramel and toast that mirror the browned onions. Serve it with luchi and the beer's fizz keeps the fried bread from feeling heavy.

Skip big IPAs with any dish that carries real chilli. High bitterness makes capsaicin feel hotter, which our guide to beer and spicy food explains.

Tomato or mango chutney is sweet and sour. A fruit beer or a gentle sour like a Berliner weisse can match the acidity, but keep the pour small.

Then the sweets. Mishti doi, sweet set yoghurt with a caramel note, goes beautifully with a milk stout or a porter. Roast and caramel meet caramel. Rosogolla is very sweet and delicate, so a light fruit beer or witbier works better than anything dark. Nolen gur sandesh, made with date palm jaggery in winter, pairs well with a Belgian dubbel, whose dried fruit and caramel notes sit close to gur. The dessert pairing guide has the general rule: the beer should be at least as sweet as the dessert.
Vegetarian plates: aloo posto and cholar dal

Aloo posto, potatoes in a paste of poppy seeds with green chilli and a little mustard oil, is creamy and nutty. A kölsch or helles matches its gentleness, while a Belgian blonde adds a soft spice that suits the poppy. Cholar dal, chana dal with coconut, raisins and a touch of sugar, is sweeter and richer. An amber lager or English bitter works well with it, especially alongside luchi.

Pour small measures, around 150 to 200 ml, so guests can try a few styles across the meal without drinking a lot. Serve lagers and wheat beers cold, near 4 to 6 °C. Serve darker ales a little warmer, around 8 to 12 °C, so their malt comes through. Keep water, nimbu pani or a good aam pora shorbot on the table for guests who do not drink.

The best way to learn this is to taste two beers side by side against one dish and notice what changes. Trained tasters do this systematically. It is a skill you can build quickly with guidance.
faqs: What is the best beer with shorshe ilish?
A hefeweizen. Its high carbonation cuts the oily fish and mustard. Its low bitterness avoids clashing with green chilli.
Does beer go with Bengali sweets?
Yes. Milk stout or porter suits mishti doi, while lighter fruit beers suit very sweet rosogolla.
Should I avoid IPA with Bengali food?
With chilli heavy dishes, yes. High hop bitterness makes chilli heat feel stronger. A gentle pale ale can work with milder dishes.
